content:
Talia Benson: Dropping ADR draft for QPL: opt-in vs default-on + where the route controls live (gateway vs routing/policy). Would love quick feedback before we stamp it. Key question: do we ever want “default-on” quantization for Hosted? And do we implement enablement checks in the API gateway layer or in routing/policy engine?

Mateo Alvarez: +1 to opt-in for v1. Default-on scares me because the failure modes are weird (workload-specific regressions, long-context perf cliffs). If we do default-on later, it should be per-org explicit setting with a canary % and a fast kill switch.

Mina Haddad: strongly prefer route-scoped. Model-scoped alone won’t work—same customer can have “interactive chat” route and “batch summarization” route, different tolerances. Also route controls need to be evaluated *after* we’ve decided the effective deployment target (GPU pool / region) bc profile compatibility depends on that.

Ravi Menon: re: where to put controls — I don’t think gateway should decide. Gateway doesn’t know hardware / kernel matrix, and it shouldn’t have to. Routing already does policy evaluation + fallback. Add quantization enablement as another policy dimension (like cost/latency tier) and have runtime do final compat check.

Nikhil Sharma: devil’s advocate: gateway is where we currently enforce request-level constraints; if this is “customer config”, would be nice to short-circuit early and return a clean error instead of routing somewhere then falling back silently.

Benji Okafor: we can still short-circuit without gateway owning the decision. Proposal: control-plane writes canonical config; policy engine evaluates and emits decision: {quantize: yes/no, canary: X, pinned_profile: optional}. Gateway just forwards. If config invalid (e.g., non-existent profile id), reject at write-time in control plane API (with audit log) not at request-time.

Priya Natarajan: +1. Gateway checks are brittle. We’d end up duplicating precedence rules in multiple places (org/customer/route overrides). If routing owns policy, we keep precedence in one engine. Also easier for Dedicated/Private parity: some deployments won’t even have the same gateway stack.

Aditya Rao: opt-in is required for launch from Product side. We need a story: “enable per route, start at 1–5% canary, watch dashboards, roll forward.” Default-on would blow up support volume.

Noah Patel: from runtime POV: routing decision isn’t sufficient anyway. Runtime still has to validate the profile is compatible with the specific worker (GPU arch, kernel availability, max seq len regime). So even if gateway says “quantize=on”, runtime might have to fall back. Better to treat gateway as not authoritative.

Sean Gallagher: SRE angle: default-on means we need aggressive auto-disable signals on every route across the fleet. For v1 we can handle opt-in + canaries. Also, gateway-based logic makes rollback harder in incidents because you’re chasing config in multiple systems.

Marcus Lin: security/compliance: please do *not* allow enabling quantization via request headers for general customers. That becomes a policy bypass path + auditing nightmare (“who turned it on?”). If we need an emergency override, keep it internal-only with RBAC, and ideally as a route config toggle that’s fully audited.

Mina Haddad: agree. If we ever do request-scoped experimentation, it should be internal debugging only (e.g., staff header) and still constrained by org policy. Otherwise customers will accidentally enable it on routes that shouldn’t be quantized.

Ethan Park: question: is the route config stored at gateway config layer today? If so, where should the canonical source live? I’d prefer control plane service -> policy engine, and gateway remains a thin auth + dispatch layer.

Ravi Menon: yep. Canonical in control plane. Routing/policy reads it (cached). Gateway doesn’t need to understand “quantization profiles” as a concept. Keeps the blast radius smaller.

Nikhil Sharma: ok, I’m convinced on “not gateway”. But we need to be explicit in ADR about user expectations: if route has quantization enabled but runtime falls back, do we surface that (metrics + response field)? Otherwise customers will think it’s “on” but they’re not getting savings.

Mateo Alvarez: good call. ADR should state: decision path is best-effort; runtime may fall back on incompatibility or load shedding; we tag traces/metrics with execution_mode=quantized|baseline and profile_id/version when applicable.

Benji Okafor: here’s a strawman config shape for ADR (route-scoped, optional customer override). Keeping it in policy engine:
```yaml
routes:
  /v1/chat/completions:
    quantization:
      enabled: true
      canary_percent: 10
      profile_policy: "auto"   # or "pinned"
      pinned_profile: null
      rollback_on_regression: true
```
Precedence: org default < customer override < route setting. All changes audited.

Talia Benson: this is great. I’ll update ADR to:
- v1: opt-in only (no default-on)
- enablement + canary evaluated in routing/policy engine (not gateway)
- runtime does final compatibility check + fallback
- no customer request headers for enablement; internal-only override (if any) with RBAC
- explicitly call out visibility: metrics/response fields reflect whether quantization actually applied
If anyone has strong objections by EOD, ping here.

Marcus Lin: +1 with the header callout. Add one sentence: “activation must be attributable to an audited config change.” :thumbsup:

Sean Gallagher: +1. Also include incident note: single kill switch at route/customer level, takes effect within cache TTL. Otherwise oncall will cry.

Talia Benson: noted. Will add TTL/propagation expectation + kill switch semantics.
